blocks.html: 7 Finiteness theorems in \(\ell\)-adic cohomology
1 Statement of the theorems
Throughout this exposé, \(S\) will be a noetherian scheme and \(A\) a left noetherian torsion ring, annihilated by an integer invertible on \(S\). Our main result is the following.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.1

We assume \(S\) regular of dimension \(0\) or \(1\). Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be a morphism of \(S\)-schemes of finite type and \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible sheaf of left \(A\)-modules on \(X\). Then the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) are constructible.
The proof will be given in section 2 and in 3.10.
1.2 Remark

In characteristic \(0\), this result is less general than [2], which proves the conclusion of the theorem for every morphism of finite type of excellent schemes of characteristic \(0\). The proof of [2] uses on the one hand resolution of singularities, and on the other hand that the schemes be of equal characteristic (in order to deduce the “purity theorem” from resolution).
1.3 Remark

We shall say that a complex \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}(X,A)\) is constructible if its cohomology sheaves are constructible, and we shall denote with an index \(c\) the subcategory of \(\mathsf{D}(X,A)\) (or \(\mathsf{D}^+\), \(\mathsf{D}^-\), \(\mathsf{D}^b\)) formed of the constructible complexes. In the language of derived categories, which we shall use freely, 1.1 says that \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast:\mathsf{D}^+(X,A) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^+(Y,A)\) sends \(\mathsf{D}_c^+\) into \(\mathsf{D}_c^+\). Let us make this explicit:

1. For \(K\) reduced to a sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) in degree \(0\), we have \(\mathscr{H}^i\mathsf{R} f_\ast K = \mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F}\); the derived statement thus implies the theorem.

  2. In the other direction, we invoke the spectral sequence

    \[ E_1^{p q} = \mathsf{R}^q f_\ast \mathscr{H}^p(K) \Rightarrow \mathscr{H}^{p+q} \mathsf{R} f_\ast K \text{.} \]

Speaking the language of derived categories has the advantage of replacing, by a simple transitivity formula \(\mathsf{R}(f g)_\ast = \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathsf{R} g_\ast\), a Leray spectral sequence \(E_2^{p q} = \mathsf{R}^p f_\ast \mathsf{R}^q g_\ast \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^{p+q} (f g)_\ast\).

Under the hypotheses of 1.1, it follows from [2] that \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast\) is of finite cohomological dimension. This allows one, in the above, to replace \(\mathsf{D}^+\) by \(\mathsf{D}\), \(\mathsf{D}^-\) or \(\mathsf{D}^b\).
1.4 The ideas of the proof

1. Poincaré duality allows one to treat the case where \(X\) is smooth, \(\mathscr{F}\) locally constant, and \(Y=S\). The dimension hypothesis appears in computing \(\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}\)'s over \(S\).

  2. We factor \(f\) as \(g j\): \(g\) proper and \(j\) an open embedding. We have \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast = \mathsf{R} g_\ast \mathsf{R} j_\ast\) and the finiteness theorem for proper morphisms controls \(\mathsf{R} g_\ast\). By dévissage, we reduce to assuming \(x\) smooth, \(\mathscr{F}\) locally constant, \(f\) an open embedding and \(Y\) proper over \(S\).

  3. An induction on \(\dim X\) (with change of \(S\)) allows one, roughly speaking, to assume the theorem true outside a part of \(Y\) finite over \(S\). Denoting by \(a:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and \(b:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) the structural morphisms, one then shows that if the theorem were false for \(\mathscr{F}\) and \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast\), it would also be false for \(\mathscr{F}\) and \(\mathsf{R} b_\ast \mathsf{R} f_\ast = \mathsf{R} a_\ast\): contradiction.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.5

Under the hypotheses of the theorem, the categories \(\mathsf{D}_c(X,A)\) and \(\mathsf{D}_c(Y,A)\) are transformed into one another by the \(4\) operations \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast\), \(\mathsf{R} f_!\), \(f^\ast\), \(\mathsf{R} f^!\).

\(\mathsf{R} f_\ast\) is treated above, \(\mathsf{R} f_!\) in [2], \(f^\ast\) is clear. There remains \(\mathsf{R} f^!\). The problem is local, which allows one to assume that \(f\) factors as \(X\xrightarrow i Z \xrightarrow g Y\) (\(i\) a closed embedding and \(g\) smooth, purely of relative dimension \(n\)). Poincaré duality \(\mathsf{R} g_! K(n)[2 n]\) and the transitivity \(\mathsf{R} f^! = \mathsf{R} i^! \mathsf{R} g^!\) reduce us to proving 1.5 for \(i\). For every \(L\in \mathsf{D}(Z,A)\), if \(j\) is the inclusion into \(Z\) of \(U=Z\setminus X\), \(i_\ast \mathsf{R} i^! L\) is the mapping cylinder of \(K\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} j_\ast j^\ast K\), and 1.5 for \(i\) follows from 1.1 for \(j\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.6

Let \(X\) be as in the theorem, and suppose \(A\) commutative. Then, if \(\mathscr{F}\) and \(\mathscr{G}\) are constructible sheaves of \(A\)-modules on \(X\), the \(\operatorname{Ext}_A^i(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G})\) are constructible: \(\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}\) sends \(\mathsf{D}_c^-(X,A)\times \mathsf{D}_c^+(X,A)\) into \(\mathsf{D}_c^+(X,A)\).

By dévissage of \(\mathscr{F}\), we reduce to assuming \(\mathscr{F}\) of the form \(j_!\mathscr{F}_1\) (\(j:Y\hookrightarrow X\) a locally closed embedding and \(\mathscr{F}_1\) locally constant on \(Y\)). We then have
\[ \mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(j_! \mathscr{F}_1,\mathscr{G}) = \mathsf{R} j_\ast \operatorname{Hom}(\mathscr{F}_1,\mathsf{R} j^! \mathscr{G}) \text{:} \]

by 1.3, we are reduced to the case where \(\mathscr{F}\) is locally constant – indeed constant, since the problem is local. For \(\mathscr{F}\) locally constant constructible, we have \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G})_x=\hom(\mathscr{F}_x,\mathscr{G}_x)\), and similarly for \(\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}\). For \(\mathscr{F}\) constant, we can therefore compute the \(\operatorname{Ext}^i\) by means of a projective resolution of finite type of its constant value, and the \(\operatorname{Ext}^i\) are constructible if \(\mathscr{G}\) is – whence the corollary.
1.7 Remark

Since \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast\) is of finite cohomological dimension, it transforms complexes of finite tor-dimension (resp. \(\leqslant d\)) into complexes of finite tor-dimension (resp. \(\leqslant d\)) [2]. [2] and the proof of 1.5 then show that finite tor-dimension is stable under the \(4\) operations \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast\), \(\mathsf{R} f_!\), \(f^\ast\), \(\mathsf{R} f^!\). A variant of that of 1.6 (dévissage of \(K\) along a partition of \(x\) to assume the cohomology sheaves locally constant, then localizing to replace \(K\) by a finite complex of locally free sheaves of finite type) then shows that, for \(A\) commutative, \(\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}\) induces

\[ \mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}:\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}^b(X,A)\times \mathsf{D}_\text{tf}^b(X,A) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}_\text{tf}^+(X,A) \]
(t.f.: finite tor-dimension).

Under the hypotheses of the theorem, the same method allows us to prove a local biduality theorem \(K\xrightarrow{\sim} D D K\) (section 4). We also prove a finiteness theorem for the sheaves of vanishing cycles. For arbitrary \(S\), one again obtains a “generic” theorem:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.9

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be a morphism of \(S\)-schemes of finite type and \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible sheaf of \(A\)-modules on \(X\). There exists a dense open \(U\) of \(S\) such that

  1. Above \(U\), the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) are constructible, and zero except for finitely many of them.

  2. The formation of the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) is compatible with every base change \(S' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\subset S\).
For \(S\) the spectrum of a field, we have \(U=S\).

If \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, a passage-to-the-limit argument yields the compatibility with \(S\)-base changes of the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast\) for every quasi-compact quasi-separated morphism of \(S\)-schemes and every sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.10

Let \(x\) be a scheme of finite type over \(k\) separably closed and \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible sheaf of \(A\)-modules. Then the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) are of finite type.
This is the special case \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(Y=S\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.11

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two schemes of finite type over \(k\) separably closed and \(K\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^-(X,A^\circ)\), \(L\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^-(Y,A)\) complexes of sheaves of right and left modules. The Künneth arrow

\[ \mathsf{R} \Gamma(X,K) \overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R} \Gamma(Y,L) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X\times Y,\mathrm{pr}_1^\ast K \overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast L) \]

is an isomorphism.
We proceed as in [2]:
\[ \xymatrix{ X\times Y \ar[r]^-{\text{pr}_1} \ar[d]^-{\text{pr}_2} & X \ar[d]^-a \\ Y \ar[r]^-b & \operatorname{Spec}(k) } \]
changing base by \(b\), we find that \(\mathsf{R}\mathrm{pr}_{2,\ast}{} \mathrm{pr}_1^\ast K\) is \(b^\ast \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,K)\). We then have (cf. [2] and its proof)

\begin{align*} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X\times Y,\mathrm{pr}_1^\ast K\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast L) &= \mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y,\mathsf{R} \mathrm{pr}_{2,\ast}(\mathrm{pr}_1^\ast K\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast L)) \\ &= \mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y,(\mathsf{R}\mathrm{pr}_{2,\ast}\mathrm{pr}_1^\ast K)\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} L) \\ &= \mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y,b^\ast \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,K)\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} L) \\ &= \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,K)\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y,L) \end{align*}
Finally, as a local counterpart to 1.9(ii), we shall prove a theorem of generic local acyclicity (2.13).
2 Generic theorems
In this section, we prove 1.9 and the theorem of generic local acyclicity 2.13. To prove 1.9, one reduces at once to assuming \(S\) integral. Let \(\eta\) be its generic point.

We shall begin by proving 1.9 under the following additional hypotheses: \(X\) is smooth over \(S\), purely of relative dimension \(n\), \(A=\mathbb{Z}/m\), \(\mathscr{F}\) is locally constant and \(Y=S\). Let \(\mathscr{F}'=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathscr{F},\mathbb{Z}/m)\). We shall show that if the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_! \mathscr{F}'\) are locally constant, the conclusions of 1.9 hold for \(U=S\). Let us recall that if \(\mathscr{L}\) is a locally constant constructible sheaf, the \(\operatorname{Ext}^i(\mathscr{L},\mathscr{G})\) are computed fibre by fibre, and are constructible if \(\mathscr{G}\) is. Let us also recall that \(\mathbb{Z}/m\) is an injective \(\mathbb{Z}/m\)-module, and is the dualizing module, so that \(\mathscr{F}=\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathscr{F}',\mathbb{Z}/m)\). Poincaré duality
\[ \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K,\mathsf{R} f^! L) = \mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathsf{R} f_! K,L) \text{,} \]
for \(K=\mathscr{F}'\), \(L=\mathbb{Z}/m\), \(\mathsf{R} f^! L = \mathbb{Z}/m[2n](n)\), thus yields
\[ \mathsf{R}^{2n-i} f_\ast \mathscr{F} = \operatorname{Hom}(\mathsf{R}^i f_! \mathscr{F}',\mathbb{Z}/m)(-n) \text{.} \]
The sheaf on the right-hand side is locally constant, of formation compatible with every base change – whence the assertion.
Let us prove 1.9 under the additional hypotheses: \(X\) is smooth over \(S\), \(\mathscr{F}\) is locally constant and \(Y=S\).

1. Decomposing \(X\) into connected components, we reduce to assuming that it is purely of a relative dimension \(n\) over \(S\).

  2. Decomposing \(A\) into a product, we reduce to assuming that \(\ell^m A=0\), with \(\ell\) a prime invertible on \(S\); we then filter \(\mathscr{F}\) by the \(\ell^k \mathscr{F}\) in order to reduce, by the corresponding spectral sequence, to the case where \(\ell\mathscr{F}=0\). We can then replace \(A\) by \(A/\ell A\) and assume that \(\ell A=0\).

  3. Replacing \(S\) by a suitable \(U\), we may assume that there exists a finite étale Galois covering \(X_1/X\), with Galois group \(G\), such that the inverse image \(\mathscr{F}_1\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X_1\) is a constant sheaf, of constant value \(F\). Denoting by \(f_1\) the projection of \(X_1\) onto \(S\), we then have

    \[ \mathsf{R}^i {f_1}_\ast \mathscr{F}_1 = (\mathsf{R}^i {f_1}_\ast \mathbb{Z}/\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/\ell} F \text{.} \]

    We also have the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence (or: the Leray spectral sequence for the covering \(X_1/X\))

    \[ \underline{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^p(G,\mathsf{R}^q {f_1}_\ast \mathscr{F}_1) \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^{p+q} f_\ast \mathscr{F} \text{.} \]

    By 2.1, we may assume, up to shrinking \(U\), that the \(\mathsf{R}^i {f_1}_\ast \mathbb{Z}/\ell\) are locally constant, of formation compatible with every base change. The same property then holds for the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F}\). Finally, if \(\overline{\eta}\) is a geometric point localized at the generic point \(\eta\) of \(S\), the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast\mathscr{F}\) are almost all zero, since the \((\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F})_{\overline{\eta}} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X_{\overline{\eta}},\mathscr{F})\) are.
Let us prove by induction on \(n\) that

blocks.label: \ast _n
blocks.html: \[ \tag{*n} \begin{array}{c} \text{The conclusions of 1.9 are true when } \dim{X_\eta}\leqslant n \\ \text{and } f \text{ is an open embedding with dense image.} \end{array} \]

For \(n=0\), up to shrinking \(S\), we have \(X=Y\): \((\ast_0)\) is obvious. Suppose (\(\ast_{n-1})\), and let us prove (\(\ast _n\)). In (\(\ast_{n-1}\)), we may replace “open embedding” by “embedding” as one sees by factoring into an open embedding and a closed embedding.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.4

Up to shrinking \(S\), the conclusions of 1.9 hold above \(Y'\subset Y\), the complement \(Y_1\) of \(Y'\) being finite over \(S\).
The assertion is local on \(Y\), which we may assume affine: \(Y\subset \mathbb{A}_S^n\). The induction hypothesis (\(\ast_{n-1}\)) applies to
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[r]^-f \ar[dr] & Y \ar[d]^-{\mathrm{pr}_i} \\ & \mathbb{A}_S^1 } \]

There thus exists, for each \(i\), a dense open \(U_i\) of \(\mathbb{A}_S^1\) such that the conclusions of 1.9 hold above \(\mathrm{pr}_i^{-1}(U_i)\); they hold above the union of the \(\mathrm{pr}_i^{-1}(U_i)\), and 2.4 follows.

Let us prove (\(\ast _n\)) for \(X\) smooth over \(S\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) locally constant on \(X\). The problem being local on \(Y\), we may assume \(Y\) affine, then projective (replace \(Y\) by its closure in a projective space). Let \(i:Y_1\hookrightarrow Y\) and \(j:Y' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be those guaranteed by 2.4.
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar@{^{(}->}[r] \ar[dr]_-a & Y \ar[d]^-b & Y_1 \ar[l]_-i \ar[dl]^-{b_1}\\ & S } \]

up to shrinking \(S\), we know that \(j^\ast \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) is constructible, of formation compatible with every base change in \(S\); we also know that \(\mathsf{R} a_\ast \mathscr{F} = \mathsf{R} b_\ast \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) is constructible, of formation compatible with every base change.
Let us apply \(\mathsf{R} b_\ast\) to the triangle defined by the exact sequence
\[ \tag{1} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & j_! j^\ast \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & i_! i^\ast \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & 0 : } \]
we obtain a triangle
\[ \tag{2} \xymatrix{ \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} b_\ast j_! j^\ast \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} a_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & (b_1)_\ast i^\ast \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & } \]

in which the first two terms are constructible, of formation compatible with every base change in \(S\) (for the first, by the finiteness theorem for the proper morphism \(b\)). The same therefore holds for the third. Since \(b_1\) is finite, we deduce that \(i^\ast \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) is constructible, of formation compatible with every base change in \(S\), and similarly for \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) by (1).

Let us prove (\(\ast _n\)) in general. We begin by reducing to the case where in \(X\) there exists a dense open \(V\) smooth over \(S\). For \(S\) the spectrum of a perfect field, it suffices to replace \(X\) by \(X_\text{red}\) (and \(Y\) by \(Y_\text{red}\)). In general, one must shrink \(S\), make a finite radicial and surjective base change \(S' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), and replace \(X\) and \(Y\) by \(X_\text{red}\) and \(Y_\text{red}\). The étale topology being insensitive to finite radicial surjective morphisms, this is harmless. Up to shrinking \(V\), we may assume \(\mathscr{F}\) locally constant on \(V\)
\[ \xymatrix{ V \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^i & X \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-f & Y . } \]
Let us define \(\Delta\) by the triangle
\[ \tag{1} \xymatrix{ \ar[r] & \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} j_\ast j^\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \Delta \ar[r] & . } \]

The cohomology sheaves of \(\Delta\) are supported in \(X\setminus V\), and \(\dim(X\setminus V)_\eta < n\). The induction hypothesis thus allows one to assume that \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast \Delta\) is constructible. Let us apply \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast\) to the triangle (1); we find a triangle
\[ \xymatrix{ \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R}(f j)_\ast j^\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} f_\ast \Delta \ar[r] & } \]
in which two of the vertices are constructible, of formation compatible with every base change in \(S\). The third is therefore so as well.

Let us prove 1.9. The problem is local on \(Y\), which we may assume affine. Taking an affine covering of \(X\) and invoking the Leray spectral sequence, we reduce to having \(X\) affine as well. All this in order to ensure that we can factor \(f\) as an open embedding followed by a proper morphism: \(f=g j\), whence \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast = \mathsf{R} g_\ast \mathsf{R} j_\ast\). The open embedding is amenable to an (\(\ast _n\)), the proper morphism to the finiteness theorem.
The following corollaries are proved as in section 1.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.9

Under the hypotheses of the theorem, for \(K\) in \(\mathsf{D}_c^b(X,A)\) or \(\mathsf{D}_c^b(Y,A)\) respectively, there exists a non-empty open \(U\) of \(S\) above which \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast K\), \(\mathsf{R} f_! K\), \(f^\ast K\), \(\mathsf{R} f^! K\) lie in \(\mathsf{D}_c^b(Y,A)\) or \(\mathsf{D}_c^b(X,A)\), and of formation compatible with every base change \(S' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\subset S\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.10

Let \(X\) be as in the theorem, and suppose \(A\) commutative. Then, if \(\mathscr{F}\) and \(\mathscr{G}\) are constructible sheaves of \(A\)-modules on \(X\), over a dense open \(U\) of \(S\), the \(\operatorname{Ext}_A^i(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G})\) are again constructible, of formation compatible with every base change \(S' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\subset S\).

If \(x\) is a geometric point of a scheme \(X\), we shall denote by \(X_x\) the strict henselization of \(X\) at \(x\). For \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and \(t\) a point geometric of \(S\), we shall denote by \(X_t\) the geometric fibre of \(X\) at \(t\). Finally, for \(x\) a geometric point of \(X\), and \(t\) a geometric point of \(S_{f(x)}\), \((X_x)_t\) is the fibre at \(t\) of \(X_x \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S_{f(x)}\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.12

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and \(K\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X,A)\). One says that \(f\) is locally acyclic at \(x\), rel. \(K\), if for every geometric point \(t\) of \(S_{f(x)}\) one has \(K_x=\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_x,K)\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{x,t},K)\). One says that \(f\) is locally acyclic, rel. \(K\), if this is true for every \(x\), and universally locally acyclic, rel. \(K\), if it remains true after every base change \(S' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.13

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a morphism of finite type and \(\mathscr{F}\) constructible on \(X\). There exists a dense open \(U\) of \(S\) above which \(f\) is universally locally acyclic, rel. \(\mathscr{F}\).
We shall admit the following result, proved in the appendix.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.14

Let \(X\xrightarrow f S_1 \xrightarrow g S_2\). If \(g\) is smooth, and \(f\) universally locally acyclic rel. \(K\), then \(g f\) is so too.
We reduce to assuming \(S\) integral, with generic point \(\eta\), and we proceed by induction on \(\dim{X_\eta}\). We begin by deducing from the induction hypothesis that

blocks.label: A
blocks.html: \[ \tag{A} \begin{array}{c} \text{Up to shrinking } S \text{, there exists } T\subset X \text{, finite over } S \text{, such that } f \\ \text{is universally locally acyclic outside } T \text{.} \end{array} \]

This question being local, we localize on \(X\) and factor \(f\) as \(X\xrightarrow u \mathbb{A}_S^1 \xrightarrow S\). The induction hypothesis applies to \(u\) and we conclude by 2.14 and the usual arguments.

To prove the theorem, we may assume \(X\) proper, since the problem is local. We shrink \(S\) so that the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) are locally constant and that (A) is applicable, and we use the following lemma.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.15

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be proper, and \(\mathscr{F}\) constructible. Suppose that the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) are locally constant and that, outside \(T\subset X\) finite over \(S\), \(f\) is locally acyclic rel. \(\mathscr{F}\). Then \(f\) is locally acyclic rel. \(\mathscr{F}\).

Let \(s\) be a geometric point of \(S\), \(S_s\) the strict localization of \(S\) at \(s\) and \(t\) a geometric point of \(S_s\). Let \(X_{(s)}\) be the inverse image of \(X\) over \(S_s\), \(\overline{j}:X_t \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_{(s)}\) and \(i:X_s \hookrightarrow X_{(s)}\). Denoting again by \(\mathscr{F}\) the inverse image of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(X_{(s)}\) or \(X_t\), we must prove that \(i^\ast \mathscr{F} \xrightarrow{\sim} i^\ast \mathsf{R} \overline{j}_\ast \mathscr{F}\). Let \(\Delta\) be the mapping cylinder of this map. Its cohomology sheaves are supported in \(T_s\). To prove that \(\Delta=0\), it therefore suffices to prove that \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,\Delta)=0\). This is the mapping cylinder of \((\mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F})_s = \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,i^\ast \mathsf{R}\overline{j}_\ast \mathscr{F}) = \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{(s)},\mathsf{R}\overline{j}_\ast \mathscr{F}) = \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_t,\mathscr{F}) = (\mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F})_t\). This specialization morphism is by hypothesis an isomorphism, and \(\Delta=0\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.16

For \(S\) the spectrum of a field, every \(S\)-scheme \(X\) is universally locally acyclic, rel. \(K\), whatever \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X,A)\) may be.
This follows from 2.13 by passage to the limit (possible, since the \(U\) of 2.13 is always equal to \(S\).

pages.title: Proof of 1.1 and constructibility of the sheaves of vanishing cycles

blocks.html: 3 Proof of 1.1 and constructibility of the sheaves of vanishing cycles

Let \(S\) be a strictly local trait (the spectrum of a henselian discrete valuation ring with separably closed residue field). We denote by \(s\) and \(\eta\) its closed and generic points, and by \(\overline{\eta}\) a geometric point localized at \(\eta\) (a separable closure of \(k(\eta)\)). Let \(X\) be over \(S\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a sheaf on \(X_\eta\). Let us recall the definition of the sheaves of vanishing cycles \(\mathsf{R}^i \Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})\) (sheaves on \(X_s\), equipped with an action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\eta}/\eta)\)). Let \(i:X_s\hookrightarrow X\), \(j:X_\eta \hookrightarrow X\), and \(\overline{j}\) the composite \(X_{\overline{\eta}}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_\eta \hookrightarrow X\); we have
\[ \mathsf{R}^i \Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}) = i^\ast \mathsf{R}^i \overline{j}_\ast (\overline{j}^\ast \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]
Here is the main theorem of this section. It improves [16].

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.2

We assume that \(X\) is of finite type over \(S\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) constructible. Then the sheaves of vanishing cycles \(\mathsf{R}^i \Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})\) are constructible.

We proceed by induction on the dimension \(n\) of \(X_\eta\). We may moreover assume – and we do assume – \(X_\eta\) dense in \(X\) (replacing \(X\) by \(\overline{X}_\eta\) does not change the \(\mathsf{R}^i \Psi\), which are supported in \(\overline{X}_\eta\)).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3

If 3.2 is true in dimension of \(X_\eta<n\), and \(\dim X_\eta=n\), there exist constructible subsheaves \(\mathscr{G}_i\) of the \(\mathsf{R}^i \Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})\) such that the supports of the local sections of \(\mathsf{R}^i\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})/\mathscr{G}\) are finite.

Let \(s'\) be a geometric generic point of the affine line over \(s\), and let \(S'\) be the strict localization at \(s'\) of the affine line \(\mathbb{A}_S^1\) over \(S\). It is again a strictly local trait, and the uniformizers for \(S\) are uniformizers on \(S'\).

\[ \xymatrix{ & \operatorname{Spec}(k') \ar[rr] \ar[dd] \ar[dr] & & (S',\eta',s') \ar[dr] \ar[dd] \\ \overline{\eta}' \ar[ur] \ar[dr] & & \mathbb{A}_{\overline{S}}^1 \ar[d] & & \mathbb{A}_S^1 \ar[dl] \\ & \overline{\eta}\ar@{^{(}->}[r] & \overline{S} \ar[r] & (S,\eta,s) } \]

Let \(k'=k(\overline{\eta})\otimes_{k(\eta)}k(\eta')\). If \(\overline{S}\) is the normalization of \(S\) in \(\overline{\eta}\), \(k'\) is the field of fractions of the strict localization of \(\mathbb{A}_{\overline{S}}^1\) at \(s'\); it is therefore a field, and \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\eta}/\eta)=\operatorname{Gal}(k'/\eta')\). Let \(\overline{\eta}'\) be the spectrum of an algebraic closure of \(k'\). The Galois group \(P=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\eta}'/k')\) is a pro-\(p\)-group, for \(p\) the characteristic exponent of \(k(s)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.4

For every scheme \(X'\) over \(S'\), and every sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X_\eta'=X_{\eta'}'\), one has, between the sheaves of vanishing cycles for \(X'/S'\) and for \(X'/S\), the relation \(\mathsf{R}^i \Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}) =\mathsf{R}^i\Psi_{\eta'}(\mathscr{F})^P\).
The following diagram compares the morphisms used in the definition of \(\mathsf{R}\Psi\) for \(X'/S'\) and \(X'/S\):

\[ \xymatrix{ X_{\overline{\eta}'} \ar[rr] \ar[d] & & X_{\eta'}' \ar@{=}[dd] \ar@{^{(}->}[dr] & & S' \\ X_{\eta'}\times_{\eta'}\operatorname{Spec}(k') \ar@{=}[d] \ar[urr] & & & X \ar[ur] \ar[dr] \\ X_\eta' \ar[rr] & & X_\eta' \ar@{^{(}->}[ur] & & S } \]
and the lemma follows from the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence, taking into account that \(P\) is a pro-\(p\)-group, with \(p\) invertible in \(A\).

Let us prove 3.3. The question is local; this allows one to assume \(X\) affine, \(X\subset \mathbb{A}_S^n\). Let \(f\) be one of the projections \(X\subset \mathbb{A}_S^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}_S^1\), \(X'\) the “localization” \(X_{\mathbb{A}_S^1} S'\) of \(x\), and \(\mathscr{F}'\) the inverse image of \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(x'\)
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{F}'\text{ on }X' \ar[r] \ar[d]^-\lambda & S' \ar[d]^-\lambda \\ \mathscr{F} \text{ on }X \ar[r]^-f & \mathbb{A}_S^1 \ar[r] & S . } \]
We have, on \(X_s'=X_{s'}'\),
\[ \lambda^\ast \mathsf{R}^i\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}) = \mathsf{R}^i \Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}') = \mathsf{R}^i\Psi_{\eta'}(\mathscr{F}')^P \text{:} \]
this sheaf is constructible, since the induction hypothesis applies to \(X'/S'\), and one uses the following lemma applied to \(X_s\subset \mathbb{A}_S^n\) and to the sheaves of vanishing cycles.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.5

Let \(\mathbb{A}^n\) be the standard affine space of dimension \(n\) over a field \(k\), \(X\subset \mathbb{A}^n\), \(]sF\) a sheaf of \(A\)-modules on \(X\) and \(\overline{\eta}\) a geometric generic point of \(\mathbb{A}^1\). Let \(X_{\overline{\eta},i}\) be the geometric generic fibre of \(X\subset \mathbb{A}^n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}_i} \mathbb{A}^1\) and \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta},i}\) the restriction of \(\mathscr{F}\) to \(X_{\overline{\eta},i}\). If the \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta},i}\) are constructible, there exists \(\mathscr{F}'\subset \mathscr{F}\), constructible, such that the local sections of \(\mathscr{F}/\mathscr{F}'\) are of finite support.
By passage to the limit, for each \(i\)

1. There exists an étale neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\overline{\eta}\) and a sheaf constructible \(\mathscr{H}\) on \(X_{U,i} = X\times_{\mathbb{A}^1,\mathrm{pr}_i} U\) whose restriction to \(X_{\overline{\eta},i}\) is \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta},i}\).

  2. For suitable \(U\), the isomorphism \(\mathscr{H}_{\overline{\eta},i} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta},i}\) comes from \(u:\mathscr{H}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}_{U,i}\) where \(\mathscr{F}_{U,i}\) is the inverse image of \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X_{U,i}\). Let \(\varphi:X_{U,i} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\). The morphism \(u\) defines \(v_i:\varphi_! \mathscr{H} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}\), with image \(\mathscr{F}_i'\). We have \((\mathscr{F}/\mathscr{F}_i')_{\overline{\eta},i} = 0\) and we take for \(\mathscr{F}'\) the sum of the \(\mathscr{F}_i'\).

Let us prove 3.2 in dimension \(n\). We may assume \(X\) affine (since the problem is local on \(X_s\)), then projective over \(S\) (take the closure of \(X\) in a projective embedding). We then have a spectral sequence [16] (the Leray spectral sequence for \(\overline{j}\), taking into account the base change theorem for the proper morphism \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\)).
\[ \tag{1} E_2^{p q} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(X_s,\mathsf{R}^i\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{p+q}(X_{\overline{\eta}},\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

Let \(\mathscr{G}^q\subset \mathsf{R}^q \Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})\) be as in 3.3, and let \(\mathscr{H}^q\) be the quotient sheaf. We have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X_s,\mathscr{H}^q)=0\) for \(i\ne 0\), and in order that \(\mathscr{H}^q\), hence \(\mathsf{R}^q\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})\), be constructible, it suffices that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X_s,\mathscr{H}^q)\) be of finite type.

Let us compute (1) modulo modules of finite type (i.e. in the quotient category of that of \(A\)-modules by the thick subcategory of \(A\)-modules of finite type). The long exact cohomology sequence deduced from \(0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}^q \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}^q\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{H}^q \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) yields, by 1.10 applied to \(\mathscr{G}^q\), that \(E_2^{p q} \sim \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathscr{H}^q)\). In particular, \(E_2^{p q}\sim 0\) for \(p\ne 0\), \(E_2^{0 q}\sim \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_{\overline{\eta}},\mathscr{F}) \sim 0\), and this completes the proof.
Parallel arguments yield the following result, which improves [16].

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.7

The formation of the sheaves of vanishing cycles is compatible with changes of trait.

Let \(g:(S',\eta',s') \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} (S,\eta,s)\) be a (surjective) morphism of strictly local traits, \(X/S\), \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X_\eta\), of torsion prime to the residue characteristic, and \((X',\mathscr{F}')\) their inverse images on \(S'\). Denoting again by \(g\) the morphisms parallel to \(g\), such as \(X_{s'}' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_s\), we must prove that
\[ \tag{3.7.1} \xymatrix{ g^\ast \mathsf{R}\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}) \ar[r]^-\sim & \mathsf{R}\Psi_{\eta'}(\mathscr{F}') . } \]
This morphism is defined by the commutative diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ X_{s'}' \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-{i'} \ar[d]^-g & X' \ar[d]^-g & X_{\eta'}' \ar[l]_-{\overline{j}'} \ar[d]^-g \\ X_s \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-i & X & X_{\overline{\eta}} \ar[l]_-{\overline{j}}} \]

A passage to the limit reduces us to assuming \(X\) of finite type over \(S\), and we proceed by induction on \(\dim{X_\eta}\). Since the question is local, we may assume \(X\) affine, then projective. Suppose (3.7.1) holds for \(\dim{X_\eta}<n\). For \(\dim{X_\eta}=n\), it then follows from the two following assertions, where \(\Delta\) is the mapping cylinder of (3.7.1).

1. The support of the local sections of the cohomology sheaves of \(\Delta\) is finite. VII:3-A

  2. \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,\Delta)=0\), hence \(\Delta=0\), by (VII:3-AA). VII:3-B

The proof of (VII:3-AA) is parallel to that of 3.3. We localize on \(X\) and consider maps \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}_S^1\); denoting by \(S(x)\) the strict henselization of \(\mathbb{A}_S^1\) at the generic point of the special fibre, we apply the induction hypothesis to \(X_1/S(x)\) (\(X_1=X\times_{\mathbb{A}^1} S(x)\)) and to \(S'(x)\). Taking the invariants under a pro-\(p\)-group, we find that \(\Delta\) is zero on the geometric generic fibre of \(X_{s'} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}_s^1\). This being true, locally on \(X\) and for every projection, we have (VII:3-AA).
For (VII:3-BB), the properness of \(X\) over \(S\) ensures that
\[ \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{s'}',\mathsf{R}\Psi_{\eta'}(\mathscr{F}')) = \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{\overline{\eta}}',\mathscr{F}') \]
and
\[ \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,\mathsf{R}\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})) = \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{\overline{\eta}},\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

We have \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,\mathsf{R}\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}))\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{s'}',g^\ast\mathsf{R}\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}))\) (invariance under change of separably closed base field); \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{s'}', \Delta)\) is therefore the mapping cylinder of \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{\overline{\eta}},\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{\overline{\eta}}',\mathscr{F}')\), an isomorphism by the same invariance theorem.

Let us prove 1.1. We reduce to assuming \(S\) connected, hence integral. If \(\dim S=0\), (\(S\) the spectrum of a field); we apply 1.9, 1.10. If \(S\) is of dimension \(1\), theorem 1.9 ensures that the \(\mathsf{R}^i f_\ast \mathscr{F}\) are constructible over the complement of a finite set \(T\) of points of \(S\). It remains to see that their restrictions to the \(Y_t\) (\(t\in T\)) are constructible. It suffices to see this after localization at \(t\): we may assume that \(S\) is a strictly local trait. The essential case is the following.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.11

Let \(X\) be of finite type over \(S\), \(j:X_\eta\hookrightarrow X\), \(i:X_s\hookrightarrow X\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) constructible on \(X_\eta\). Then, \(i^\ast\mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathscr{F}\) is constructible.

Let \(I=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\eta}/\eta)\) be the inertia group. We know that it is an extension of \(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}_{p'}(1)\) by a pro-\(p\)-group \(P\) (\(p\) the characteristic exponent of the residue field). The Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence gives
\[ E_2^{p q} = \mathscr{H}^p(I,\mathsf{R}^q\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F}))\Rightarrow i^\ast \mathsf{R}^{p+q}j_\ast\mathscr{F} \text{.} \]

Let \(R_t^q = \mathsf{R}^q\Psi_\eta(\mathscr{F})^P\) (\(t\) for tame). If \(\sigma\) is a generator of \(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}_{p'}(1)\), we have \(E_2^{0 q} = \ker(\sigma-1,R_t^q)\), \(E_2^{1 q} = \operatorname{coker}(\sigma-1,R_t^q)\) and \(E_2^{p q} = 0\) for \(p\ne 0,1\). These sheaves are constructible, since the sheaves of vanishing cycles are, and 3.11 follows.

Let us treat the general case, \(S\) still being a strictly local trait. If \(X=X_\eta\), \(f\) is the composite \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_\eta \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) and we apply 1.9 and 3.11. In the general case, let \(j:X_\eta\hookrightarrow X\) and let \(\Delta\) be the mapping cylinder of \(\mathscr{F} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} j_\ast j^\ast \mathscr{F}\). Its cohomology sheaves have support in \(X_s\); by 1.9 applied to \(X_s \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_{s'}\), \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast \Delta\) is therefore constructible. The complex \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathsf{R} j_\ast j^\ast \mathscr{F} = \mathsf{R}(f j)_\ast j^\ast \mathscr{F}\) is also so, and we conclude by the triangle
\[ \xymatrix{ \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathsf{R} j_\ast j^\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} f_\ast \Delta \ar[r] & . } \]
4 Local biduality

Let \(S\) be regular of dimension \(0\) or \(1\) and set \(K_S=A\) (constant sheaf of value \(A\)). For \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}^b(S,A)\), we set \(D K=\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K,K_S)\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(S,A^\circ)\) (a complex of sheaves of right \(A\)-modules). We still have \(D K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}^b(S,A^0)\), and an explicit computation, possible because \(S\) is of dimension \(1\), shows \(K\xrightarrow{\sim} D D K\) (for \(A=\mathbb{Z}/n\), [V]Duality 1.4).

We will assume that \(A\) is commutative, a hypothesis no doubt unnecessary. For \(a:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) of finite type over \(S\), we set \(K_X=\mathsf{R} a^! K_S\). For \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}^b(S,A)\), we set \(D K=\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K,K_X)\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}^b(X,A)\). Our main result is the following

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.3

We have \(K\xrightarrow{\sim} D D K\) (\(K\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\textnormal{ctf}^b(X,A)\)).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.4

If \(a\) is proper, we have \(\mathsf{R} a_\ast K \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R} a_\ast D D K\).
Poincaré duality
\[ \mathsf{R} a_! \mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K,\mathsf{R} a^! K_S) = \mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathsf{R} a_! K,K_S) \]
furnishes us with an isomorphism \(\mathsf{R} a_\ast D = D \mathsf{R} a_! = D \mathsf{R} a_\ast\). The lemma follows from the commutativity of the diagram ([V]Duality, 1.2)
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R} a_\ast K \ar[r] \ar[d]^-\wr & \mathsf{R} a_\ast D D K \ar[d]^-\wr \\ D D \mathsf{R} a_\ast K \ar[r]^-\sim & D \mathsf{R} a_\ast D K . } \]

One sees by localization that it suffices to treat the cases where \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, or a trait. For \(S\) the spectrum of a field, we proceed by induction on \(\dim X\). Since the problem is local, we may assume \(X\) proper. Moreover, the induction hypothesis ensures, by the usual arguments, that the mapping cylinder \(\Delta\) of \(K\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} D D K\) has skyscraper cohomology sheaves. The lemma then ensures that \(\mathsf{R} a_\ast \Delta=0\), hence that \(\Delta=0\).

For \(S\) a trait, we already know that 4.3 holds on the generic fibre (4.5). We may also assume \(X\) proper over \(S\) and we proceed by induction on \(\dim{X_s}\), \(X\) proper over \(S\). The mapping cylinder \(\delta\) again has skyscraper cohomology sheaves, on \(X_s\), and we conclude as above.

Suppose that \(A=\mathbb{Z}/m\). We then have a variant of the preceding theory, taking \(K\) arbitrary in \(\mathsf{D}_c^b(X,A)\). The complex \(\mathsf{R} a^! \mathbb{Z}/m\) is of finite injective dimension [2]. This ensures that \(D K\) is again in \(\mathsf{D}_c^b(X,A)\). To prove local biduality over \(S\), we use that \(\mathbb{Z}/m\) is the dualizing \(\mathbb{Z}/m\)-module. Then we proceed as before.
5 Appendix, by L. Illusie

In this appendix, which takes up certain parts of the late [21], and a letter from P. Deligne to the author, we prove 2.14 as well as various generalizations and variants of the specialization theorems [2] and ([I]Étale cohomology 5.1.7).

The schemes and morphisms considered will be assumed quasi-compact and quasi-separated. If \(X\) is a scheme and \(x\) a geometric point of \(X\), we will denote by \(X(x)\) the strict localization of \(X\) at \(x\).
We fix a base scheme \(S\) and a sheaf of rings \(A\) on \(S\) (not necessarily commutative nor noetherian). If \(X\) is an \(S\)-scheme, we will write \(\mathsf{D}(X)\) for \(\mathsf{D}(X,A_X)\).
5.1 Cohomological properness

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.1.1

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be an \(S\)-morphism and \(E\in\operatorname{Ob} \mathsf{D}^+(X)\). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. The formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast E\) commutes with every finite base change \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\).

  2. The formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast E\) commutes with every quasi-finite base change (or projective limit of quasi-finite morphisms) \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\).

  3. For every specialization arrow \(i:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) ([I]Étale cohomology, 5.1.2), if one denotes by \(\widetilde S\) the normalization in \(k(\overline{t})\) of the integral scheme closure of \(i(t)\) in \(S(s)\) (by [20]) \(\overline{S}\) is thus local integral, with closed point radicial over \(s\)), \(\overline{f}:\overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{Y}\) the morphism deduced from \(f\) by the base change \(\overline{S}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), \(f_s:X_s\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_s\) the fibre of \(f\) at \(s\), then the base change arrow

    \[ (\mathsf{R} \overline{f}_\ast (E|\overline{X}))|Y_s \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} {f_s}_\ast(E|X_s) \]

    is an isomorphism.

The equivalence of (i) and (ii) follows from Zariski's main theorem, and it is clear that (ii) implies (iii). Let us prove that (iii) implies (ii). For every \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), projective limit of quasi-finite morphisms, and every point geometric \(s\) of \(S'\), let us denote by \(C(S',s)\) the cone of the base change arrow
\[ (\mathsf{R} f_\ast'(E|X'))|Y_s \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}{f_s}_\ast (E|X_s) \text{,} \]

where \(f':X'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y'\) is the morphism deduced from \(f\) by the base change \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and \(f_s:X_s\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_s\) the fibre of \(f\) at \(s\). We must prove that, for every \((S',s)\) as above, \(C(S',s)\) is acyclic. We will show, by induction on \(N\), that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i C(S',s) = 0\) for \(i\leqslant N\). By the Main Theorem, passage to the limit, and cleaning up of radicial morphisms, we may assume that \(S\) and \(S'\) are strictly local, \(S'\) integral, with closed point \(s\), \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) finite. Let \(t\) be a generic geometric point of \(S'\), and \(\overline{S}\) the normalization of \(S'\) in \(k(t)\). Let \(\overline{S}_\bullet\) be the coskeleton simplicial scheme of \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S'\) (\(\overline{S}_0=\overline{S}\),…\(\overline{S}_n=(\overline{S}/S')^{n+1}\),…), \(X_\bullet=X\times_S \overline{S}_\bullet\). \(g_\bullet:\overline{X}_\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X'\) the canonical projection. Let us set \(G|X'=G'\). The bicomplex \({g_\bullet}_\ast g_\bullet^\ast G'\), with columns the \({g_n}_\ast g_n^\ast G'\), is a resolution of \(G'\) [2]. We may thus represent \(C(S',s)\) by a bicomplex whose columns are identified with the \(C(\overline{S}_n,s)\). By (iii), \(C(\overline{S}_0,s)=C(\overline{S},s)\) is acyclic. On the other hand, for \(n>0\), we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S}_n,s)=0\) for \(i\leqslant N\) by the induction hypothesis. We conclude that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i C(S',s)=0\) for \(i\leqslant N+1\), which completes the proof.
Let \((f,E)\) satisfy condition (i) of 5.1.1.

1. If \(E\in \operatorname{Ob} \mathsf{D}^b(X)\), and \(f_\ast\) is of finite cohomological dimension, then, for every \(F\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^-(S,A^\circ)\), the canonical arrow

    \[ \tag{*} \mathsf{R} f_\ast(E)\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_A q^\ast F \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} f_\ast(E\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_A p^\ast F) \text{,} \]

    where \(p:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), \(q:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) are the projections, is an isomorphism. Same conclusion with \(E\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^-(X)\).

By dévissage, it indeed suffices to verify the assertion for \(F\) of the form \(i_! A_{S'}\), with \(i:S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) quasi-finite. By the Main Theorem, we reduce to assuming \(i\) finite; the conclusion is then equivalent to the commutation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast(E)\) with base change by \(i\).
1. We assume \(A\) noetherian, constructible. Then, for every \(F\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^b(S,A^\circ)\), constructible and of finite tor-dimension, the arrow (*) above is an isomorphism.

We reduce indeed, by dévissage, to the case where \(F\) is of the form \(i_! M\), with \(i:S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) locally closed, \(A\) locally constant on \(S'\), \(M\) constructible, of finite tor-dimension, and with locally constant cohomology on \(S'\). Changing base from \(S\) to \(S'\), we are thus reduced to the case where \(F\) is perfect [5], hence finally, by localization and dévissage, to the case where \(F=A\), for which the conclusion is trivial.

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be an \(S\)-morphism, and \(E\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X)\). We will say that \((f,E)\) is cohomologically proper rel. to \(S\) if the formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast E\) commutes with every base change \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\). It amounts to the same to say that after every base change \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), the formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast' E'\) (where \(f'=f\times_S S'\), \(E'=\)inverse image of \(E\) on \(X\times_S S'\)) commutes with every finite base change \(S'' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S'\) (cf. [2]). Here are some examples of cohomological properness (for a study of the analogous notion for sheaves of sets or of non-commutative groups, the reader is referred to [23]).

1. We assume \(A\) of torsion and \(f\) proper. Then, for every \(E\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X)\), \((f,E)\) is cohomologically proper rel. to \(S\) (proper base change theorem, [2]).

  2. We assume \(S\) finite, \(X\) and \(Y\) of finite type over \(S\), and \(A\) annihilated by an integer invertible on \(S\). Then, for every \(E\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X)\), \((f,E)\) is cohomologically proper rel. to \(S\) (1.9).

  3. We assume \(A\) constant, noetherian, annihilated by an integer \(n\) invertible on \(S\), \(f:X=Y\setminus D\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) the inclusion of the complement of a divisor \(D\) on \(Y\), with normal crossings rel. to \(S\) [23]. Let \(E\) be a sheaf of \(A\)-modules on \(X\) satisfying one of the following conditions:

    1. \(E\) is locally constant constructible and tamely ramified along \(D\);

    2. \(E\) is, locally for the étale topology on \(Y\) and on \(S\), the inverse image of a sheaf of \(A\)-modules on \(S\).

    Then \((f,E)\) is cohomologically proper rel. to \(S\), and \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast E\) constructible (compare with [23]).

Let us sketch the proof in case (i). The question is local in the neighbourhood of a point \(y\) of \(Y\). We may assume \(D\) a sum of smooth divisors, \(D=\sum_{i=1}^m D_i\). By virtue of the relative Abhyankar lemma [23], we may, in the neighbourhood of \(y\), trivialize \(E\) by a finite covering \(\widetilde Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) of the form \(\widetilde Y=Y[T_1,\dots,T_r]/(T_1^{n_1}-t_1,\dots,T_r^{n_r}-t_r)\) where the \(t_i\) are local equations of the smooth divisors passing through \(y\), and the \(n_i\) integers prime to the char. of \(k(y)\). The inverse image \(\widetilde D\) of \(D\) in \(Y\) is again with normal crossings rel. to \(S\), and if \(g:\widetilde X=\widetilde Y\setminus \widetilde D\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is the projection, \(g^\ast E\) is constant. Since \(E\) injects into \(g_\ast g^\ast E\) and the quotient is tamely ramified, an easy dévissage reduces to the case where \(E\) is constant. Let us denote by \(p:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), \(q:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) the projections, and, for \(1\leqslant i\leqslant m\), \(f_i:Y\setminus D_i \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} D\) the canonical inclusion. From the relative purity theorem [2] we easily deduce, by induction on \(m\), that, for every \(A\)-module locally constant \(M\) on \(S\), the canonical arrow
\[ \tag{5.1.3.1} \mathsf{R} f_\ast (\mathbb{Z}/n)\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} q^\ast M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} f_\ast (p^\ast M) \]
is an isomorphism, and that on the other hand we have:
\begin{align*} \tag{5.1.3.2} {f_i}_\ast(\mathbb{Z}/n) &= \mathbb{Z}/n \text{,} \\ \mathsf{R}^1 {f_i}_\ast (\mathbb{Z}/n) &= (\mathbb{Z}/n)(-1)_{D_i} \text{,} \end{align*}
a canonical isomorphism being given by the fundamental class \(\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\) ([IV]Cycle 2.1.4),

\begin{align*} \mathsf{R}^q {f_i}_\ast(\mathbb{Z}/n) &= 0\text{ for } q>1 \text{,} \\ \mathsf{R} f_\ast (\mathbb{Z}/n) &= \bigotimes_i^\mathsf{L} \mathsf{R} {f_i}_\ast (\mathbb{Z}/n) \text{ , i.e.:} \\ \mathsf{R}^1 f_\ast(\mathbb{Z}/n) &= \bigoplus_{i=1}^m (\mathbb{Z}/n)(-1)_{D_i} \text{,} \\ \textstyle\bigwedge^\bullet \mathsf{R}^1 f_\ast(\mathbb{Z}/n) &\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}^\bullet f_\ast (\mathbb{Z}/n) \text{.} \end{align*}

The conclusion of 3, in case (i), thus follows from (5.1.3.1) and (5.1.3.2). In case (ii), we reduce, by passage to the limit, to the case where \(E=p^\ast M\), with \(M\) constructible, then, by dévissage and base change (using (i)), to the case \(M\) constant, already treated.
It follows from the preceding proof that (5.1.3.1) is an isomorphism for every \(M\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(S)\).

One will compare formulas (5.1.3.2) with the analogous formulas in integral cohomology in the case \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C})\) (see for example [12]), which follow from the fact that, locally for the classical topology, the complement of \(D\) has the homotopy type of a torus.

By passage to the limit, we deduce from (5.1.3.2) formulas similar in \(\ell\)-adic cohomology, i.e. with \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) replaced by \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\) (\(\ell\) a prime number invertible on \(S\)). Suppose \(q:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) proper and smooth. It then follows from the Weil conjectures [14, 15] that the Leray spectral sequence
\[ E_2^{i j} = \mathsf{R}^i q_\ast \mathsf{R}^j f_\ast \mathbb{Z}_\ell \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^\bullet p_\ast \mathbb{Z}_\ell \]
degenerates at \(E_3\) modulo torsion [11]. The same phenomenon occurs in integral cohomology in the case \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C})\), see (loc. cit.) and [12].
5.2 Specialization and cospecialization
Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and \(E\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X)\).

Suppose that the formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast E\) commutes with every finite change of base. For every specialization \(u:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) of geometric points of \(S\), one then defines an arrow, called the specialization arrow,
\[ \tag{5.2.1.1} \operatorname{sp}(u):\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,E|X_s) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_t,E|X_t) \text{,} \]

in the following manner. Let, as in 5.1.1(iii), \(\overline{S}\) be the normalization in \(k(t)\) of the closure of \(u(t)\) in \(S(s)\), and \(\overline{f}:\overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{S}\) the morphism deduced from \(f\) by the base change \(\overline{S}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\). By the trivial part (i)\(\Rightarrow\)(iii) of 5.1.1, the base change arrow

\[ \tag{5.2.1.2} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(\overline{X},E|\overline{X})=\mathsf{R}\overline{f}_\ast (E|\overline{X})_s \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,E|X_s) \]
is an isomorphism. One defines (5.2.1.1) as the composite of the inverse of (5.2.1.2) and the restriction arrow
\[ \tag{5.2.1.3} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(\overline{X},E|\overline{X}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_t,E|X_t) \text{.} \]

Suppose that \(f\) is locally acyclic rel. to \(E\) (2.12). For every specialization \(u:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) of geometric points of \(S\), one then defines an arrow, called the cospecialization arrow,
\[ \tag{5.2.2.1} \operatorname{cosp}(u):\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_t,E|X_t) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,E|X_s) \text{,} \]

defined in the following manner. Let \(g:X_t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), \(g':\overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be the canonical arrows. It follows from the local acyclicity hypothesis that the canonical arrow
\[ \tag{5.2.2.2} \mathsf{R} g_\ast'(E|\overline{X})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} g_\ast(E|X_t) \]

is an isomorphism. Indeed, we may assume \(S\) strictly local, integral, with closed point \(s\), \(t\) being a generic geometric point. Let us compute the fibre of (5.2.2.2) at a point geometric \(x\) in \(X\), with image \(y\) in \(S\). Replacing \(S\) by the strict localization of \(S\) at \(y\) if need be, we may assume that \(y=s\). Since \(\overline{S}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is a projective limit of finite morphisms, and radicial at \(s\), we find that \(\mathsf{R} g_\ast'(E|\overline{X})_x = E_x\) and that the fibre of (5.2.2.2) at \(x\) is identified with the restriction \(E_x=\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x),E)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x)_t,E|X(x)_t)\), which is an isomorphism by hypothesis. Applying \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,-)\) to (5.2.2.2), we deduce that the restriction arrow (5.2.1.3) is an isomorphism. One defines (5.2.2.1) as the composite of the inverse of (5.2.1.3) and the base change arrow (5.2.1.2).
If \(s'' \xrightarrow{u'} s' \xrightarrow u s\) are the specialization arrows of geometric points of \(S\), one verifies that one has
\begin{align*} \operatorname{sp}(u')\operatorname{sp}(u'') &= \operatorname{sp}(u u') \text{,} \\ \operatorname{cosp}(u) \operatorname{cosp}(u') &= \operatorname{cosp}(u u') \text{,} \end{align*}
each time that both sides are defined.

Suppose that the formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast E\) commutes with every finite change of base, and that \(f\) is locally acyclic rel. to \(E\). It follows from the definitions that, for every specialization \(u:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) of geometric points of \(S\), the arrows \(\operatorname{sp}(u)\) and \(\operatorname{cosp}(u)\) are isomorphisms, inverse to one another.

The preceding hypotheses are satisfied notably when \(A\) is noetherian, annihilated by an integer \(n\) invertible on \(S\), \(f\) proper and smooth, and \(E\) with locally constant cohomology (cohomological properness of proper morphisms (5.1.3), and local acyclicity of smooth morphisms [2]). We recover the “specialization theorem” [2].
On the other hand, 5.1.1 has the following consequence:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.5

Suppose that \(f\) is locally acyclic relative to \(E\), and that, for every specialization \(u:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\), the cospecialization arrow \(\operatorname{cosp}(u)\) is an isomorphism. Then the formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast E\) commutes with every finite base change.
Taking 5.2.4 into account, 5.2.5 generalizes ([I]Étale cohomology 5.1.7).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2.6

Suppose that \(f\) is locally acyclic rel. to \(E\). Let \(x\) be a geometric point of \(X\), with image \(s\) in \(S\); let us denote by \(f_{(x)}:X(x)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) the morphism induced by \(f\). Then the formation of \(\mathsf{R} {f_{(x)}}_\ast(E|X(x))\) commutes with every finite base change \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\).

It suffices, by 5.2.5, to verify that the cospecialization arrows for \((f_{(x)},E|X(x))\) are isomorphisms. By transitivity of the cospecialization arrows (5.2.3), it suffices to show that, if \(u:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) is a specialization, then \(\operatorname{cosp}(u):\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x)_t,E|X(x)_t)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x)_s,E|X(x)_s)\) is an isomorphism. But, since \(s\) is closed in \(S(s)\), \(X(x)_s\) is strictly local with closed point \(x\), \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x)_s,E|X(x)_s)=E_x\), and \(\operatorname{cosp}(u)\) is an isomorphism, inverse of the restriction isomorphism \(E_x\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x)_t,E|X(x)_t)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2.7

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be an \(S\)-morphism, \(p:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), \(q:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) the projections, and \(E\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X)\). Assume \(A\) locally constant, \(f\) locally acyclic rel. to \(E\), and \(q\) locally acyclic at every geometric point \(y\) of \(Y\) rel. to every sheaf locally constant in the neighbourhood of \(y\). Then \(p\) is locally acyclic rel. to \(E\).

Let \(x\) be a geometric point of \(x\), with images \(y\) and \(s\) in \(Y\) and \(S\), \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) a specialization, \(f_{(x)}:X(x)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y(y)\) the morphism induced by \(f\). We must show that the restriction
\[ \tag{*} E_x \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x)_t,E|X(x)_t) \]
is an isomorphism. We may assume \(A\) constant. By 5.2.4 and 5.2.5, for every specialization \(z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y(y)\), the specialization arrow
\[ E_x = \mathsf{R} {f_{(x)}}_\ast (E|X(x))_y \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} {f_{(x)}}_\ast (E|X(x)|_z = \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x)_z,E|X(x)_z) \]
is an isomorphism, in other words \(\mathsf{R}{f_{(x)}}_\ast(E|X(x))\) is constant of value \(E_x\). The acyclicity hypothesis on \(q\) thus implies that the restriction
\[ E_x \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(Y(y)_y,(E_x)|Y(y)_t) = \mathsf{R}\Gamma\left(Y(y)_t,\mathsf{R} {f_{(x)}}_\ast (E|X(x))|Y(y)_t\right) \]
is an isomorphism. But this arrow is identified with (*), whence the conclusion.

The hypothesis of 5.2.7 on \(q\) is satisfied notably when \(q\) is smooth, and \(A\) is annihilated by an integer \(n\) invertible on \(S\) [2]. On the other hand, if the hypotheses of 5.2.7 are satisfied after every base change \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), one then concludes that \(p\) is universally locally acyclic rel. to \(E\). From these remarks follows in particular statement 2.14.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2.8

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and \(E\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X)\). Assume that \(f\) is universally locally acyclic rel. to \(E\), that the formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast E\) commutes with every finite base change, and that for every morphism \(s'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} s\), where \(s\) is a geometric point of \(S\) and \(s'\) the spectrum of a separably closed field, the base change arrow \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,E|X_s)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{s'},E|X_{s'})\) is an isomorphism. Then \((f,E)\) is cohomologically proper (5.1.3).

Let \(f':X'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S'\) be the morphism deduced from \(f\) by a base change \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\); we must see that the formation of \(\mathsf{R} f_\ast'(E|X')\) commutes with every finite base change. By 5.2.5, it suffices to show that, for every specialization \(u':t'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S'(s')\), the arrow of cospecialization \(\operatorname{cosp}(u')\): \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{t'}',E|X_{t'}') \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{s'}',E|X_{s'}')\) is an isomorphism. Let \(s\) (resp. \(t\)) be the geometric point image of \(s\) (resp. \(t\)) in \(S\), \(u:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) the specialization defined by \(u'\). One easily sees that one has a commutative square

\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_t,E|X_t) \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{cosp}(u)} \ar[d] & \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_s,E|X_s) \ar[d] \\ \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{t'}',E|X_{t'}') \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{cosp}(u')} & \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X_{s'}',E|X_{s'}') } \]

where the vertical arrows are the base change arrows. By hypothesis, these are isomorphisms. On the other hand (5.2.4) \(\operatorname{cosp}(u)\) is an isomorphism, hence \(\operatorname{cosp}(u')\) is an isomorphism, which completes the proof.

Here is an example of application of 5.2.8. Suppose \(A\) annihilated by an integer \(n\) invertible on \(S\), \(f\) locally of finite type and universally locally acyclic. Let \(x\) be a geometric point of \(X\), with image \(s\) in \(S\), \(f_{(x)}:X(x)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\) the morphism induced by \(f\). It follows from 5.2.6 and 1.9 (by passage to the limit) that the hypotheses of 5.2.8 are satisfied by the pair \((f_{(x)},E|X(x))\), which is therefore cohomologically proper.

Suppose \(A\) constant. Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\), and \(E\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(X)\) the complex of finite tor-dimension. We will say that \(f\) is strongly locally acyclic rel. to \(E\) if, for every geometric point \(x\) of \(X\), with image \(s\) in \(S\), every specialization \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S(s)\), and every \(A^\circ\)-module \(M\), the restriction arrow
\[ E_x\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_A M \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X(x)_t,(E|X(x)_t)\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_A M) \]
is an isomorphism. I do not know whether “locally acyclic” implies “strongly locally acyclic.”

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.10

Under the hypotheses of 5.2.9, suppose \(A\) noetherian of torsion, \(S\) noetherian, and \(f\) strongly locally acyclic rel. to \(E\). Then, for every diagram with cartesian squares

\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]^-f & X' \ar[d]^-{f'} \ar[l]_-j& X'' \ar[d]^-{f''} \ar[l]_-{j'}\\ S & S' \ar[l]_-i& S'' , \ar[l]_-{i'}} \]

with \(i\) quasi-finite and \(i'\) an open immersion, and every \(F\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^+(S'',A^\circ)\), the canonical arrow

\[ \tag{*} j^\ast E \overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} {f'}^\ast \mathsf{R} i_\ast' F \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} j_\ast' ((j j')^\ast E\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} {f''}^\ast F) \]

is an isomorphism.
One will compare this statement with [2].

Let us prove 5.2.10. We easily reduce to \(S=S'\), strictly local, and \(F\) constructible, concentrated in degree \(0\). We then resolve \(F\) on the right by finite sums of sheaves of the form \(u_\ast M\), where \(u:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is a geometric point and \(M\) an \(A^\circ\)-module. The hypothesis implies that (*) is an isomorphism for \(F=u_\ast M\), whence the result.
